rewrites.summary:
Documents and screening: federal document and airport policy applies — the federal airport-security framework (body-scanner flags and pat-downs, documentation mismatches, requesting alternative screening) governs any traveller, and the 2025–26 federal turn is felt through it (marker disputes, screening friction) with no local statute to soften it.

Legal protections: nothing criminalises trans status or conduct, no anti-trans enforcement or care ban appears in the audited record, and same-sex marriage is legal — a 2015 territorial court ruling struck down licence denials — so marriage and partner travel face no recognition barrier. Protection, however, rests on an attorney-general's 2017 interpretation that the human-rights law's sex provision covers transgender students, not on legislation.

Practical safety: the community numbers tens of thousands across three main islands, so everyday recognition risk is high; the local posture is quietly protective rather than hostile.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Parent-state policy turbulence colours the record: the 2025–26 federal turn is felt through federal document and airport policy (marker disputes, screening friction) with no local statute to soften it — a federal rollback that sits above a thin but genuinely welcoming local posture.

Same-sex marriage became legal through a 2015 territorial court ruling that found the licence denial unconstitutional — the resident marriage baseline — and the historic sodomy statute (1957 application) is superseded.

rewrites.summary:
Federal document, immigration and screening policy applies, including 2025–26 marker restrictions; nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression.

Marriage recognition reached the islands in 2015 by operation of the federal constitution, so partner travel faces no recognition barrier; the 2023 legislature enacted a hate-crimes statute whose sentencing criteria expressly cover sexual orientation and gender identity — a formal, if recent, protection.

Visitor reality: no documented legal danger, a fresh hate-crime shield, minimal other institutional support, and high social visibility in small, church-influenced island communities.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent policy flux: the 2025–26 federal turn includes marker restrictions applied through federal document, immigration and screening policy, while marriage recognition arrived by operation of the federal constitution rather than local legislation — national framework above, local posture below.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The comprehensive national equality index scores the commonwealth's gender-identity law as negative and the sexual-orientation law as 'low', citing family-law gaps — no second-parent adoption, no assisted-reproduction recognition, no family-services protection; protections beyond federal law are limited to government employees, and gender-marker changes require a specified medical process.

Community life is visible and peaceful: the first Pride event drew a crowd of about 60 people, and the first same-sex marriage was officiated in July 2015.

rewrites.summary:
Criminal law: male same-sex acts were criminalised under the 1969 Crimes Act (terms to seven or ten years, consent no defence) until parliament repealed the provisions in April 2023, effective 1 June 2023. Enforcement in living memory was essentially absent, so the repeal removed a held-over risk rather than an active prosecution threat.

Legal protections: no marriage equality and no general non-discrimination statute; same-sex marriage remains outlawed, so marriage and partner travel have no local recognition path.

Practical safety: public life is strongly church-inflected, and with a population of some 15,000 everyone is known — decriminalised, unequal, and small.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Legislative flux: a decade of stalled bills, drafting assisted by its partner New Zealand, preceded the April 2023 repeal — a contested path rather than a quick legislative turn.
rewrites.localsOnly: Pre-contact history reframes the present: 2020 coverage noted a nation 'historically accepting of same-sex relationships' whose anti-LGBT sentiment arrived with colonial administration. The repeal followed sustained advocacy by the local Te Tiare Association, whose spokespeople called the old laws 'draconian' colonial relics.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: In free association with New Zealand; local deviations noted above. Population figures vary across the audited sources — roughly 15,000 in the record text, 21,000 in a 2017 source; the church-inflected climate's practical weight for an outed visitor is unquantified.

rewrites.summary:
Criminal law: colonial-era offences were removed and the age of consent was reportedly equalised by 2011; no audited source documents enforcement against queer people at all; equally there is no recognition of same-sex relationships and no non-discrimination statute.

Documents and screening: legacy public-health law provided for HIV testing of visitors staying beyond about two months — rarely invoked, but on the books.

Practical safety: with a small population near 1,500, anonymity is impossible — the question is community reaction, not arrest, and it is quietly unresolved.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The legal chain is colonial inheritance: the offences were inherited from partner New Zealand via 1901 annexation, retained on self-governance in 1974, and survived the 1986 decriminalisation of its partner New Zealand itself.
rewrites.localsOnly: Culturally, UN regional documentation lists the fakafifine among the region's pre-colonial third-gender identities — 'cultural treasure' framing that signals deep family embedding, coexisting with church-led conservatism. The principal 1966 act still shows uneven ages of majority by sex (21 men/19 women) on its face into the 2010s.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: In free association with New Zealand; local deviations noted above. Community reaction to an outed visitor is quietly unresolved in the audited record, and the legacy HIV-testing provision, while on the books, has undocumented application.

rewrites.summary:
Same-sex conduct is not criminalised. Documents and screening: the apex court ruled in 2023 that full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a precondition for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card — a reversal of a 2019 high-court loss in the same litigation — so a functioning marker-change route exists on cards; beyond the card, recognition still runs on surgery.

Legal protections: no relationship recognition and no SOGI equality ordinance; in September 2025 the legislature voted down the government's own registered-partnerships bill 71–14.

Practical safety: no criminal law and dense urban anonymity, inside a system that still demands surgery for most recognition and whose politicians recently voted inclusion down.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Litigation flux shaped the record: the 2023 apex ruling reversed a 2019 high-court loss in the same litigation, and the September 2025 vote of 71–14 landed after court deadlines — the executive chose against where it had discretion; an earlier landmark ruling (2006) had established equal age of consent.
rewrites.localsOnly: Corporate visibility invites backlash: a bank's rainbow installations drew a homophobic campaign in 2016. Open activism operates in a space tightened since the 2020 security law.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Special administrative region of China; local deviations noted above. Beyond the identity card, recognition still runs on full surgery, and the ruling's reach beyond cards is unresolved in the audited record.

rewrites.summary:
Criminal law and documents: nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression; no legal gender-recognition pathway exists, so identity documents cannot be changed — a trans man holding a card issued elsewhere remains registered female locally, with border-crossing confusion as the practical consequence.

Legal protections: near zero — no recognition of same-sex unions, and protection exists only in employment law; a 2016 domestic-violence law knowingly excluded same-sex partners as non-'family', against a 2015 international direction that protection be non-discriminatory.

Practical safety: zero legal risk and near-zero legal recourse, in the compression of a very small city where casinos, churches and old resident networks all know their own; the administration treats the subject as a non-issue — which is both the mercy and the void.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Governance and policy trajectory: a small southern territory with its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation; the first organised push (2015) got only a hearing; the 2026 official position is that recognition still needs 'prudent study', with no plans to revise the framework, despite a March 2026 appeal by four trans residents — the territory remains the only area in China without an ID gender-marker or sex-reassignment path, both available elsewhere in the country.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing record: same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1996; the constitutional discrimination list omits sexual orientation; the only protection is employment-only; a 2012 domestic-violence draft dropped same-sex cohabitants for 'lack of social consensus'; the first ID-marker push (2015) got only a hearing, the claimant speaking behind a screen. The exclusion of same-sex partners from the 2016 domestic-violence law drew public accusation against the administration, warning it signals that SOGI bias is justifiable.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of China; local deviations noted above. The 2026 official statement leaves reform timing unset; the employment-only protection's enforcement practice is undocumented; the April 2026 appeal by four trans residents has no reported outcome in the audited material.

An overview: same-sex activity decriminalised in 1996; no recognition of same-sex unions; the constitution's discrimination list omits sexual orientation; protection only in employment law (2008); a 2012 domestic-violence draft dropped same-sex cohabitants for 'lack of social consensus'; a 2015 gender-marker-change study never produced a law.

News reporting (September 2023): trans residents cannot change sex on ID cards — no data-change policy exists — causing border-crossing confusion (a trans man holding a card marked male elsewhere is still registered female locally); activists press the long-promised legislative reform.

News reporting (April 2026): the justice services office says gender-identity legal recognition still needs 'prudent study' of core societal values, civil and family law, and says there are 'no plans to revise the framework' — the only area in the parent nation without ID gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions, both possible elsewhere, despite a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents.

rewrites.summary:
Criminal law: same-sex intimacy is criminalised — six months to three years — with wide police discretion, and morality articles are the tool turned on visibly trans people; the penal code of the administering state governs any visitor.

Documents and screening: rights reviews document involuntary outing, expression discrepancies at checkpoints and registries, no gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition — a 2021 path covers intersex people only — and the religious establishment of the administering state has condemned transition.

Practical safety: enforcement is a live danger — 170 charged in the administering state in one year, a 2020 organised outing campaign — and for an outed visitor the exposure is criminalisation, morality enforcement and occupation policing, with no civil space and negligible accountability.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Governance context: the disputed North African territory sits under military administration by a neighbouring state; a 2017 legality roundup records the partially recognised claimant administration as likewise criminalising same-sex conduct.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing record: rights defenders have been tried at the territory's own court — a 2005 case of eight Sahrawis remains a landmark; a 2018 legal study recorded LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike; and a 2020 organised outing campaign struck at residents' identity.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Disputed territory administered by the neighbouring state; local deviations noted above; see the entry on the administering state for the underlying legal analysis.
